ai.definition: Quantum Cryptography Systems utilize the principles of quantum mechanics, particularly the properties of qubits, to provide an unbreakable method of encryption. This technology ensures that any attempt at eavesdropping will be detected, thus maintaining absolute data security.
ai.howItWorks: Qubits are used in quantum cryptography systems for secure transmission and verification of information. The unique properties of these quantum states allow for the creation of a shared secret key between two parties, which can then be used to encrypt and decrypt messages. Any interception or measurement of this key by an eavesdropper will cause a disturbance that is immediately detectable by both communicating parties.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional cryptographic methods are vulnerable to quantum computing attacks, where powerful enough quantum computers could potentially break current encryption algorithms. Quantum cryptography provides a solution by leveraging the laws of quantum mechanics to ensure secure communication even against quantum adversaries.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves creating and manipulating qubits using various technologies such as superconducting circuits, trapped ions, or photons. These qubits are then integrated into secure communication networks through specialized hardware and software.
ai.buildProcess: Building a quantum cryptography system requires expertise in quantum physics, materials science, and cybersecurity. The process includes designing the quantum devices, implementing error correction protocols, and integrating these components with classical communication infrastructure.
ai.costDrivers: High costs are driven by the need for ultra-low noise environments, specialized cooling systems, and complex control electronics. Additionally, the scarcity of skilled personnel in this emerging field contributes to higher development and operational expenses.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is promising as governments and financial institutions recognize the importance of quantum-proof security solutions. However, widespread adoption faces challenges related to technological maturity and cost.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still evolving, but there is growing interest from government bodies to standardize and regulate quantum cryptography systems due to their critical role in national security and data protection.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the fragility of qubits and susceptibility to environmental noise. Market risks involve high initial costs and potential obsolescence if quantum computers become widely available before full commercialization is achieved.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to the early stage of development and high initial investment required. However, as security threats increase, there could be significant demand from government and enterprise sectors willing to invest in robust security solutions.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments will likely focus on improving qubit coherence times, reducing error rates, and integrating quantum cryptography into larger secure communication networks. Additionally, advancements in miniaturization and integration with classical systems are expected to drive down costs and enhance usability.

glossary.def: A quantum bit that can exist in multiple states simultaneously, enabling the processing of complex information.
A method for securely distributing cryptographic keys using principles of quantum mechanics to ensure security.

subsystems.name: Photon source
subsystems.role: emits the single photons or heavily attenuated laser pulses that carry each key bit.

subsystems.name: Quantum channel and detectors
subsystems.role: the link where any eavesdropping necessarily disturbs the quantum states, plus the detectors that record them.
parts: single-photon detectors (semiconductor avalanche or superconducting nanowire)

subsystems.name: Classical authenticated channel
subsystems.role: public, non-secret traffic used to compare measurements, correct errors and prove the sifted key is genuine.

subsystems.name: Post-quantum algorithm suite
subsystems.role: software-only encryption and signatures whose security rests on mathematical problems believed hard for quantum computers.

subsystems.name: Protocol integration
subsystems.role: slots the new keys into the channels people actually use.
parts: hybrid TLS 1.3 handshake (classical Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman plus ML-KEM)

subsystems.name: Range extenders
subsystems.role: carry keys beyond the roughly 100–200 km a single fibre span allows.

buildSteps.title: Fix the threat model
buildSteps.detail: Decide whether you need hardware key distribution, software-only quantum-resistant algorithms, or both, and how long the protected data must stay secret.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate detectors
buildSteps.detail: Semiconductor single-photon avalanche diodes are made on doped wafers; superconducting nanowire detectors are patterned as nanometre-wide meanders and later cooled to a few kelvin.

buildSteps.title: Align the optical module
buildSteps.detail: Laser, modulator and fibre couplers are positioned to sub-micron tolerance, bonded, sealed and temperature-stabilised.

buildSteps.title: Build the key pipeline
buildSteps.detail: Raw detections are sifted, error-corrected and privacy-amplified, with every classical message authenticated, until both ends hold identical secret bits.

buildSteps.title: Implement the post-quantum algorithms
buildSteps.detail: ML-KEM and ML-DSA are coded in constant time, checked against the published standard test vectors, and fuzzed and probed for side-channel leaks.

buildSteps.title: Hybridise and integrate
buildSteps.detail: The classical and post-quantum exchanges run together in one TLS handshake, so a break in either alone does not expose the session.

buildSteps.title: Roll out
buildSteps.detail: Browsers, servers, VPN gateways and certificate authorities are upgraded, with monitoring so an old client cannot quietly negotiate a weaker mode.

buildSteps.title: Operate and monitor
buildSteps.detail: Key rate and detector noise are watched for signs of interception, while the algorithm suite is tracked against advances in cryptanalysis.

prerequisites.why: quantum key distribution cannot work without devices that emit and register individual photons reliably.

prerequisites.tech: Low-loss optical fibre and free-space links
prerequisites.why: photons lost in transit cannot carry key material.
lattice and hash-based schemes were published as US federal standards in 2024, giving vendors something stable to implement.
algorithms are only as strong as the code and hardware that run them; timing and power leaks remain a live risk.
without them, key distribution is limited to single fibre spans or chains of trusted nodes that must themselves be physically secure.

pathway.milestone: hybrid classical-plus-post-quantum handshakes are switched on in mainstream browsers, and metro-scale quantum key links operate in a few countries
pathway.unlocks: protection of today's traffic against future decryption of recorded data.

pathway.milestone: post-quantum certificates and signatures replace classical ones across certificate authorities and long-lived devices
pathway.unlocks: end-to-end quantum-resistant authentication, not just key agreement.

pathway.milestone: satellite and inter-city quantum links extend key distribution beyond single fibre spans
pathway.unlocks: national-scale key delivery where trusted relay nodes are unacceptable.

pathway.milestone: repeater-based quantum networks and device-independent protocols
pathway.unlocks: key security that rests on measured physics rather than on trusting the hardware vendor.
